ayvalik-kite-beach.description: A resort town in the north of the Turkish Aegean, opposite Lesbos. Two spots: Kite Beach with a kite station and restaurant, and the Causeway on the road to Cunda Island — glassy “speed” water in offshore wind. The northerly summer wind blows from about mid-June to mid-September, the most reliable months being July and August. The riding area stretches for more than 5 km.
ayvalik-kite-beach.rating_basis: IKSURFMAG calls Ayvalık “Turkey's secret spot” and the Causeway “one of the best flat-water spots we've found”; Aaron Hadlow and Sam Light have ridden here
ayvalik-kite-beach.waves_note: Flat, shallow, clear water at both spots; no waves or shorebreak
ayvalik-kite-beach.hazards: Offshore wind at the Causeway; the Kite Beach → Causeway downwinder only as an organised trip with locals
ayvalik-kite-beach.gustiness_note: With a light northerly forecast and +28–30 °C heat — a 12 m day; on normal days 7–9 m; up to ~30 kn
ayvalik-kite-beach.crowd_note: According to IKSURFMAG — “really only a few kiters around”

Almost empty on the water
Inexpensive, quiet resort with good food
cons: Short season (mid-June to mid-September)
Causeway — offshore wind and no infrastructure
Far from İzmir (~2.5 h)
ayvalik-kite-beach.wind_dir: N (Meltemi), side / side-onshore at Kite Beach; offshore at the Causeway
ayvalik-kite-beach.airport: EDO — Edremit, ~40 min; ADB — İzmir, ~2.5 h

urla-gulbahce.description: Gülbahçe Bay (Çarpan) near Urla is the first kite spot on the way from İzmir to the Çeşme Peninsula, about 30 minutes short of Alaçatı. Shallow, lagoon-like water and the northerly summer wind make it a handy place to learn; on the shore there are several schools with rentals, cafés and showers. There are three launch points: the southwest shore (schools), the east shore (side-shore) and a shallow spit in the north.
urla-gulbahce.rating_basis: The closest kite spot to İzmir, with flat shallow water and several schools (kitejungle); reviews say it's less windy than Alaçatı but easier for learning
urla-gulbahce.waves_note: An enclosed bay: flat water or light chop, no waves; glassy water for speed at the northern spit
urla-gulbahce.hazards: Offshore, gusty wind at the northern spit; lots of students around the schools
urla-gulbahce.gustiness_note: Northerly summer wind plus a daytime thermal; at the northern spit the wind is offshore and gusty
pros: Shallow flat water — easy to learn
Close to İzmir and the airport
Several schools and rentals
cons: Lighter and less steady wind than in Alaçatı
Northern spit — offshore wind, experienced riders only
urla-gulbahce.wind_dir: N (Poyraz / Meltemi), side-shore on the east shore; strong offshore at the northern spit

zanzibar-paje.description: A snow-white beach in southeast Zanzibar with a huge, shallow, reef-protected lagoon. Two seasons: the northerly Kaskazi (Dec–Feb) and the stronger southeasterly Kusi (Jun–Sep). Riding depends entirely on the tide: at low water the inner lagoon dries out and everyone moves to the outer lagoon and the sandbanks.
zanzibar-paje.rating_basis: IKSURFMAG: knee-deep flat lagoons, two wind seasons, warm water, dolphins and turtles; downsides — heavy tide dependence, sea urchins and seaweed farms
zanzibar-paje.waves_note: Inner and outer lagoons — knee-deep flat water (tide-dependent); chop and kickers at high tide; waves on the reef ~1–2 km out
zanzibar-paje.hazards: Sea urchins (booties needed), coral on the reef, seaweed farms, currents at the reef pass, shallows at low tide
zanzibar-paje.gustiness_note: The monsoon winds are steady; the Kusi is lighter in the morning and builds in the afternoon
zanzibar-paje.crowd_note: Paje is Zanzibar's main kite centre, and the lagoon is busy in season (especially at low tide, when everyone moves to the outer lagoon)
zanzibar-paje.region: East coast of Zanzibar (Unguja), Indian Ocean
pros: Warm water, 25–29 °C — no wetsuit needed
Knee-deep flat water — ideal for learning
Two wind seasons a year
Dolphins, turtles, beach parties, Stone Town
cons: Riding is tied to the tides
Sea urchins and seaweed farms
Rainy season (April–May) with almost no wind
Crowded in peak season
zanzibar-paje.wind_dir: Kaskazi — NE (Dec–Feb), Kusi — SE (Jun–Sep); side-shore / side-onshore

cape-hatteras-waves.description: The Outer Banks are a narrow chain of barrier islands between the Atlantic and Pamlico Sound. On the sound side there are endless waist-deep flat-water shallows, ideal for learning and freestyle; on the ocean side, waves. The centre of the kite scene is the village of Waves, with the REAL Watersports kite resort and the Real Slick park. The best months are May and September–October; winter is windy but cold.
cape-hatteras-waves.rating_basis: The main kite resort on the US East Coast: windy months all year round, the huge shallow flat-water lagoon of Pamlico Sound; kickers and sliders at Real Slick (REAL Watersports)
cape-hatteras-waves.waves_note: On the Pamlico Sound side — a huge shallow area with flat water and chop, no shorebreak; waves on the island's ocean side
cape-hatteras-waves.hazards: Hurricanes and storms (June–November), thunderstorms as fronts pass through, jellyfish and crabs in the shallows in summer, sliders and kickers in the kite park
cape-hatteras-waves.gustiness_note: An open barrier island: the wind is steady (the IKSURFMAG author — “the most consistent wind in a long time”); the direction changes with the season and the fronts
cape-hatteras-waves.crowd_note: Busy around the kite centres in spring and autumn, but there are enough shallows for everyone; most water access is via private paths
pros: Huge flat-water shallows
Wind at any time of year
Ocean waves too
Good for learning
cons: Cold water and air in winter
Lighter wind and heat in summer
A long drive from the airports (~2–2.5 h from Norfolk)
cape-hatteras-waves.wind_dir: SW in summer, NE/N in autumn and spring; usually side-shore at Real Slick
cape-hatteras-waves.airport: ORF — Norfolk, ~2–2.5 h; MQI — Dare County (general aviation), ~30 min

corpus-christi-packery-channel.description: Packery Channel is a shallow spot on the Laguna Madre side of North Padre Island: knee- to waist-deep flat water and a grassy bottom. Corpus Christi is famous for its constant summer southeasterly; the main season is May–September, but you can ride year-round. Around it are a dozen other spots (Wildcat, North Beach, Oso Bay, Fish Pass).
corpus-christi-packery-channel.rating_basis: Local riders call Corpus Christi the “holy grail” for having the most rideable days in the US; kiteboarding.com: SE 17–21 mph all summer
corpus-christi-packery-channel.waves_note: Knee- to waist-deep flat water; sometimes waves on the ocean side by the jetty
corpus-christi-packery-channel.hazards: Oyster shells (booties a must), the boat channel in the canal, seaweed; on the ocean side — stay 200 yards from the north jetty
corpus-christi-packery-channel.gustiness_note: The summer SE is steady (thermals over land strengthen the flow); the frontal northerly in winter is gusty
corpus-christi-packery-channel.crowd_note: Lots of spots within 30 min — kiters are spread out
pros: Lots of windy days
Shallow flat water, good for learning
Many alternative spots nearby
cons: Cold fronts in winter, gusty N and cool water
Booties needed because of oyster shells
Kiting is banned in Padre Island National Seashore (Bird Island Basin)
corpus-christi-packery-channel.wind_dir: SE in summer (side-onshore), N with cold fronts in winter

hood-river.description: A small town in the Columbia River Gorge — North America's summer capital of kiting and windsurfing. Wind from the Pacific accelerates through the gorge and blows almost every day from May to September. The main launches are the sandbar at the mouth of the Hood River and the Event Site; the water is dense chop and river swell running against the current. Fresh water, the Mount Hood volcano on the horizon and plenty to do on windless days.
hood-river.rating_basis: North America's cult river spot: strong wind almost every summer day (usually 18–25 mph, IKSURFMAG), lots of spots along the gorge (Stevenson, Rufus) and a well-developed kite culture
hood-river.waves_note: Dense river chop at the Event Site, flat water downstream behind the sandbar; in strong wind against the current a river swell builds (bigger and cleaner at Rufus, 45 miles east)
hood-river.hazards: Strong river current (sweeps you downstream if you crash), a shipping channel with barges, cold water in spring and autumn, slippery rocks at the Stevenson and Rufus launches
hood-river.gustiness_note: The summer wind “blows through” the Columbia Gorge from the west: strong and often gusty; steadier at Stevenson
hood-river.crowd_note: The Event Site is the busiest launch in the gorge — crowded in summer, with hotels fully booked at weekends; quieter upstream
pros: Wind almost every day June–August
Fresh water, no salt or jellyfish
Lots of spots along the gorge
Great infrastructure and things to do on windless days
cons: The water is cool even in summer — wetsuit needed
Gusty and crowded
Strong current and barges — not for complete beginners

maui-kanaha-kite-beach.description: Kanaha Beach next to Kahului airport is the heart of Maui's kite scene, where many tricks and brands were born. The trade wind blows almost every day from spring to autumn; there's chop near shore and quality waves on the outer reef, big in winter. Beginners are taught at neighbouring Teach Beach; the kite zones are restricted because of the nearby airport.
maui-kanaha-kite-beach.rating_basis: The birthplace of modern kitesurfing and one of the world's wave meccas: leading brands and riders are based at Kite Beach (Naish Beach); IKSURFMAG — windy months March–October, trade wind 15–25 mph
maui-kanaha-kite-beach.waves_note: Chop and a small shorebreak near shore, lines of waves on the outer reef, overhead in winter swells; at Kihei in the south — waves in a south swell
maui-kanaha-kite-beach.hazards: Shallow reef (dangerous if you fall), shorebreak, powerful swell in winter; sharks and turtles possible; respect the kite zone boundaries near the airport
maui-kanaha-kite-beach.gustiness_note: The trade wind blows a steady 15–25 mph on most days from spring to autumn; in winter the wind is less reliable, with occasional southerly “Kona” winds
maui-kanaha-kite-beach.crowd_note: Kite Beach is the island's main spot, and the reef gets crowded in good wind; lessons are held separately at Teach Beach
pros: Steady trade wind April–September
World-class reef waves
Warm water and Hawaiian nature
10 minutes from the airport
cons: Reef and waves — not a place for beginners
Expensive (accommodation, car)
Restricted riding zones because of the airport

el-yaque.description: A village in the south of Margarita Island, known for decades as the world capital of windsurfing, and later of kiting. A huge shallow bay with chop and a side-shore trade wind suits both beginners and freestylers, and boat trips to Coche Island offer perfectly flat water. The resort is half-empty these days — fewer people, but weaker infrastructure; schools arrange transfers and trips to Araya and La Restinga.
el-yaque.rating_basis: A legendary Caribbean windsurf/kite spot with shallow warm water and wind “almost all year round” (IKSURFMAG); today almost free of crowds because of the situation in Venezuela; Russian-language roundups mention Venezuela as the best winter destination
el-yaque.waves_note: No waves at El Yaque — light chop, waist-deep far from shore; perfectly flat water at Coche Island (20 min by boat or a 15 km downwinder); waves at La Restinga
el-yaque.hazards: Gusty wind in the afternoon, offshore wind at Coche (the school boat provides backup), shells on La Restinga beach; safety: don't rent a car, use school transfers, check foreign ministry travel advice
el-yaque.gustiness_note: Trade wind almost every day, but it can be gusty after midday; at Coche the wind is offshore and picks up by 10 a.m.
el-yaque.crowd_note: IKSURFMAG: “you won't find crowded spots these days”; windsurfers and kiters share the beach
pros: Shallow warm water far from shore
Wind almost every day from February to July
Uncrowded water
Trips to the flat water of Coche and Araya
cons: Complicated logistics: no direct international flights (via Caracas)
The political and crime situation in Venezuela
Gusty after midday
el-yaque.airport: PMV — Porlamar (Margarita), ~40 min; international flights via CCS Caracas

mui-ne.description: Mui Ne is Vietnam's main kite resort and one of the most Russian-speaking kite places in Asia: dozens of schools along Ham Tien beach, including some with Russian instructors (MKS, KiteFamily, KITENAM and others). From November to March a strong northeast monsoon blows, boosted by thermals. Besides the main beach there's Malibu (waves), Harbour Wall (flat water), Suối Nước and Turtle Island; 3–4 h to the north is the Phan Rang lagoon.
mui-ne.rating_basis: One of Asia's best-known kite resorts (Figaro Nautisme names Mui Ne among Asia's top destinations); a steady monsoon November–March, strong wind and waves, lots of schools; downsides — crowding and shorebreak at high tide
mui-ne.waves_note: On the main beach — shorebreak and 1–2 m waves, up to 2–3 m in strong wind in December–February; Malibu — waves and onshore wind; by the Harbour Wall and at Secret Spot — the only flat water in the area
mui-ne.hazards: Strong shorebreak at high tide, erosion and a narrow beach in the northern part of Rang Beach, a rocky headland by Ganh Beach and at the Cemetery spot, crowds and people ignoring right-of-way rules, jellyfish (low risk), strong sun
mui-ne.gustiness_note: The monsoon is boosted by thermals: 10–15 kn in the morning, 20–25 by midday, 25–30+ in the afternoon; gusty at Harbour Wall after 13:00 and at Turtle Island
mui-ne.crowd_note: Crowded on the main beach in December–January, sometimes 30–40 kites on a single stretch; Suối Nước and Malibu are quieter
pros: Steady, strong wind November–March
Lots of schools, including Russian-speaking ones
Warm water year-round, cheap accommodation and food
Several spots for every style: waves, flat water, ~15 km downwinders
cons: Shorebreak and a narrow beach at high tide — a tricky launch for beginners
Crowded on the main beach in peak season
The wind in December–February is often 25–30+ kn — hard for beginners
Litter on some beaches (Malibu, Harbour Wall)
mui-ne.airport: SGN — Ho Chi Minh City, ~4–5 h by car (also CXR — Cam Ranh, ~4 h)

phan-rang-my-hoa.description: My Hoa lagoon by the village of My Tan is the main kite spot in Ninh Thuan Province and the windiest place in Vietnam. An outer reef about 1 km offshore breaks the waves: inside there's shallow flat water for learning, freestyle and speed, and outside the reef there are waves. A small kite village with several schools and kite hotels has grown up around the lagoon; many people come here on camps from Mui Ne.
phan-rang-my-hoa.rating_basis: Described as having stronger, steadier wind than Mui Ne, with a flat lagoon behind the reef; Phan Rang Kite Center — 4.8 on Google (344 reviews) and 5.0 on Tripadvisor; it hosted a Kiteboard Tour Asia event (2016, ~100 riders)
phan-rang-my-hoa.waves_note: Inside the lagoon, sheltered by a reef about 1 km from shore — flat water and light chop; outside the reef — waves for wave riding (experienced riders only). In summer the main spot is Ninh Chu Bay, with flat shallow water
phan-rang-my-hoa.hazards: Coral rubble, sharp shells and rocks at low tide (booties needed), a sudden drop-off at the edge of the bank, the reef and waves beyond it, rapidly strengthening afternoon wind; typhoons possible in May
phan-rang-my-hoa.gustiness_note: One of the windiest areas in Vietnam: the monsoon is boosted by the mountains, averaging ~20–25 kn in season, rarely below 15, sometimes up to 35–40; steadier than in Mui Ne
phan-rang-my-hoa.crowd_note: Much less crowded than Mui Ne: 10–20 riders on a good day, up to a few dozen kites over the lagoon in peak season
phan-rang-my-hoa.region: Ninh Thuan Province (My Tan / Ninh Hai), ~20 km northeast of Phan Rang
pros: Strong, steady monsoon, steadier wind than in Mui Ne
Flat shallow water in the lagoon
Few people compared with Mui Ne
Accommodation 50 m from the launch, Cam Ranh airport ~1 h away
cons: Heavily tide-dependent: coral and rocks are exposed at low tide
Wind often 25+ kn — beginners are better off in the morning
Little infrastructure or entertainment beyond kiting
Small choice of rental gear
phan-rang-my-hoa.wind_dir: N–NE (northeast monsoon), side / side-onshore; S–SSE at Ninh Chu in summer

cape-town-bloubergstrand.description: The Blouberg–Table View coast north of Cape Town, with views of Table Mountain, is a mecca for big air and wave riding. A strong southeasterly blows almost daily from November to March, the water is cold (13–15 °C), and there's a choice of beaches: from the relatively flat Dolphin Beach to the waves of Sunset and Calmers. A great city, wine and nature for windless days.
cape-town-bloubergstrand.rating_basis: One of the world's top destinations for big air and waves: IKSURFMAG — 20–40 knots ~5 days a week from December to February, a dozen beaches along the coast, downwinders with views of Table Mountain
cape-town-bloubergstrand.waves_note: Chop and kickers almost everywhere; Dolphin Beach has the flattest water at high tide; Sunset Beach and Calmers — clean waves, big in a swell; strong shorebreak at Doodles
cape-town-bloubergstrand.hazards: Cold water, strong gusts, shorebreak (Doodles, Sunset), rocks at Big Bay and north of Calmers, currents; theft from cars in car parks
cape-town-bloubergstrand.gustiness_note: The southeasterly “Cape Doctor” is strong and regular but comes in surges near Table Mountain; it picks up by ~10:00 and peaks by 16:00
cape-town-bloubergstrand.crowd_note: In December–February the whole kite world descends; crowded at Big Bay, Dolphin Beach (school groups) and Calmers; November and March are quieter
pros: Strong, regular wind in the southern summer
Wide choice of beaches and waves
World-class downwinders and big air
Cape Town: food, wine, nature
cons: Cold water — 4/3–5/4 mm wetsuit
The wind is often too strong for beginners
Crime: don't leave things in the car, be careful in the evening
Long-haul flight

langebaan-lagoon.description: A long (≈15 km) enclosed lagoon on South Africa's West Coast, part of West Coast National Park. The southerly summer wind blows along the shore over flat or slightly rippled water — a great place for learning and freestyle when Cape Town is too windy or too wavy. The water is noticeably warmer than in Table Bay.
langebaan-lagoon.rating_basis: The Western Cape's main flat-water spot: a long shallow lagoon in West Coast National Park where freestylers train (mentioned in IKSURFMAG's Cape Town guide); the water is warmer than at Table View
langebaan-lagoon.waves_note: The lagoon is closed off from the ocean — no waves; flat in the shallow zones, chop in strong wind
langebaan-lagoon.hazards: Currents at the lagoon outlet when the tide turns, nature conservation zones (part of the water is closed), strong sun
langebaan-lagoon.gustiness_note: The same southerly summer wind as in Cape Town, but over flat terrain — steadier and without the “surges” off the mountains
langebaan-lagoon.crowd_note: Shark Bay is busy in December–January, but the lagoon is long — you can move along the shore
langebaan-lagoon.region: Western Cape, West Coast, ~1.5 h north of Cape Town
pros: Flat water with no waves
Steadier wind than in Cape Town
Good for beginners and freestylers
Warmer water than at the ocean beaches
cons: 1.5 h from Cape Town — car needed
Little entertainment in the town
In winter (May–September) the wind is light and it's cold

bells-beach.description: Bells Beach is the legendary right-hand reef on the Surf Coast near Melbourne and home of the world's oldest professional surf contest. Powerful open walls rolling in from the Southern Ocean (the Rincon and Bowl sections) work on SW swells and a NW offshore; the best time is March–September. The water is cold (13–18 °C), so you need a 4/3–5/4 wetsuit in winter.
bells-beach.rating_basis: “Australia's most iconic right” (The Surf Atlas): a reef point with the Rincon and Bowl sections, home of the oldest professional contest — the Rip Curl Pro Bells Beach (a WSL CT event, traditionally held at Easter). Surf-forecast notes highly consistent swell from autumn to spring
bells-beach.hazards: Rocky (sandstone) reef, strong currents under the break and towards Jan Juc on big days, cold water, powerful sets on a big swell; sharks in the region (low risk)
bells-beach.crowd_note: Crowded when it's on, especially at weekends (Melbourne is 1.5 h away); Winkipop is even tighter, with a stricter pecking order; quieter on winter weekdays
bells-beach.region: Victoria, Surf Coast (Torquay, start of the Great Ocean Road), Bass Strait / Southern Ocean
bells-beach.area_breaks: Nearby: Rincon and Bowl (sections of Bells), Winkipop (long right, experienced surfers), Jan Juc (beach break, all levels, currents on big days), Torquay Point and Torquay Surf Beach (learning), Point Addis, Anglesea (beginner beaches)
bells-beach.beginner_months: Beginners learn on the Torquay beaches (Torquay Surf Beach) and Jan Juc, and at Anglesea; in summer (December–February) the waves are smaller and the water warmer — easier for learning
pros: Iconic right-hand point with powerful walls
Consistent Southern Ocean swell from autumn to spring
Torquay next door — birthplace of Rip Curl and Quiksilver, every surf shop you need
Lots of breaks along the Great Ocean Road
cons: Cold water and air in winter
Often small and onshore in summer
Crowded at weekends
Not for beginners
bells-beach.airport: AVV — Avalon, ~40 min; MEL — Melbourne, ~1.5 h

byron-bay-the-pass.description: Byron Bay is a surf town with a hippie vibe on the easternmost point of Australia. The Pass is a soft, long right off Cape Byron, perfect for longboarding, and around the bay there are beaches and points for every level. In summer and autumn easterly and cyclone swells arrive; in winter big SE swells hit the exposed beaches.
byron-bay-the-pass.rating_basis: Australia's iconic longboard point: a soft, long right (150–200 m) off Cape Byron, with a dozen beaches and points nearby. Guides (The Surf Atlas) call it one of the most enjoyable spots in the country; Surf-forecast reviews ~3/5 because of the crowds
byron-bay-the-pass.hazards: Crowds, longboards and SUPs on the take-off, rocks at the cape, strong currents at Main Beach and Belongil on a big winter swell, sharks (especially Tallows), bluebottles (Portuguese man o' war) in summer
byron-bay-the-pass.crowd_note: The Pass is almost always packed with longboarders, SUPers and students, with jostling on the take-off; Wategos, Tallows and Broken Head are quieter
byron-bay-the-pass.region: New South Wales, North Coast (Cape Byron), Pacific Ocean
byron-bay-the-pass.area_breaks: Nearby: Wategos (north-facing beach, a left — rare for NSW, longboarding), Clarkes Beach (right-hand point, sheltered from southerly wind), Main Beach and The Wreck (peaks by the shipwreck, intermediate+), Tallows (the most consistent beach break, sharks), Broken Head (point, 15 min south), Lennox Head (powerful right-hand point, 20 km south)
byron-bay-the-pass.beginner_months: Year-round: schools teach at Clarkes Beach and Main Beach and on the inside section of The Pass when it's small; in summer (November–March) the waves are usually smaller and softer — easier for beginners
pros: Long, soft rights — longboard heaven
Spots for every level within a few kilometres
Plenty of schools, rentals and surf culture
Warm water most of the year
cons: Very crowded at The Pass
Sharks — there have been serious incidents in the area
Expensive accommodation
Frequent NE onshore in spring
byron-bay-the-pass.airport: OOL — Gold Coast, ~50 min; BNK — Ballina, ~30 min

gold-coast-snapper-rocks.description: Snapper Rocks is the start of the Superbank, an artificially pumped sandbar off Point Danger on the Queensland–New South Wales border. On E and SE swells long right-hand walls and barrels run from Snapper to Greenmount, and sometimes all the way to Kirra. Warm water, a well-developed city, a WSL event — and one of the most crowded line-ups in the world.
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.rating_basis: The Superbank is one of the world's best-known right-hand waves: a sandbar from Snapper to Kirra (record rides of 1–2 km), with an annual WSL Championship Tour event. Surf-forecast reviews 5/5; the main drawback is crowds of up to hundreds of people and fights over waves
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.hazards: Crowds and board collisions, rocks at Snapper point, backwash and a strong current along the sandbar — hard to hold position on the peak, localism; sharks in Australia (low risk overall, nets in place), stinging bluebottles in the summer NE wind
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.crowd_note: One of the most crowded line-ups in the world: on a good day up to several hundred surfers at Snapper, constant drop-ins. Greenmount is always packed; quieter on the beaches further north (Burleigh, Currumbin) or at dawn on weekdays
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.region: Queensland, southern Gold Coast (Coolangatta / Rainbow Bay), Coral Sea / Pacific Ocean
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.area_breaks: Along the Superbank: Snapper Rocks → Rainbow Bay → Greenmount → Coolangatta → Kirra (a famous barrel on a big swell). Nearby: Duranbah (beach break by the Tweed breakwall, picks up any swell, locals), Currumbin Alley, Burleigh Heads (right-hand point), Surfers Paradise and Main Beach (beach breaks)
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.beginner_months: Year-round on the inside sections of Coolangatta and Rainbow Bay when it's small, and on the beaches at Kirra and Currumbin; on big swell days the points are no place for beginners
pros: World-class long right-hand barrels
Cyclone season (January–April) and winter swells deliver waves most of the year
A city with full infrastructure, airport close by
Many spots for different levels along the coast
cons: Huge crowds and aggressive competition
Localism at Snapper and Duranbah
The sandbar constantly shifts — quality is unpredictable
Frequent NE onshore and small surf in spring (September–November)
gold-coast-snapper-rocks.best_wind_dir: S–SE (southeasterly, offshore for the right-hand points)

margaret-river-main-break.description: Main Break (Surfers Point) at the mouth of the Margaret River is a powerful reef A-frame: a long left and a short, steep right, working from double overhead up to 6 m on swells from the Roaring Forties. It hosts a WSL event and is the heart of a surf region with dozens of reefs and beaches along the wine coast. The water is cool (17–21 °C), so a wetsuit is a must.
margaret-river-main-break.rating_basis: Western Australia's premier wave and a WSL Championship Tour venue (Margaret River Pro); guides (Surfertoday, The Surf Atlas) describe a powerful world-class reef A-frame that holds waves up to 6 m. The region is one of the most swell-consistent in the world
margaret-river-main-break.hazards: Powerful waves and heavy sets, shallow reef and rocks, a long paddle out to the line-up (up to 20 min), strong currents on a big swell, great white sharks (a higher-risk region)
margaret-river-main-break.crowd_note: Main Break gets crowded on a good swell, but when it's big only experienced surfers stay out; at neighbouring spots (South Point, Gallows, The Farm) the crowd depends on weekends and school holidays
margaret-river-main-break.region: Western Australia, Margaret River region (Prevelly), Indian Ocean
margaret-river-main-break.area_breaks: Nearby: The Bombie (big wave, tow-in), The Box (barrelling right over shallow reef, experts), Southside, North Point and South Point at Gracetown, Gallows, Lefthanders, Injidup, Yallingup (Supertubes), Three Bears (Baby Bear for learning), Redgate and Gnarabup (beaches)
margaret-river-main-break.beginner_months: Lessons run year-round on sheltered beaches — Gracetown, Redgate, Gnarabup, Baby Bear (Three Bears) and the Margaret River mouth; in summer (December–February) the waves are smaller and mornings are offshore — easier for beginners
pros: One of the most consistent swells in the world
World-class waves at dozens of spots
Empty spots on weekdays outside school holidays
Nature, wine and a national park all around
cons: The main break is for experienced surfers only
Cool water, a 3/2–4/3 wetsuit needed
Sharks — there have been fatal attacks in the region
Strong southerly sea breeze in summer afternoons
margaret-river-main-break.airport: PER — Perth, ~3 h; BQB — Busselton (Busselton-Margaret River), ~45 min

barbados-soup-bowl.description: Soup Bowl in Bathsheba is a powerful right over coral and limestone reef on Barbados's wild Atlantic coast, one of the most consistent waves in the Caribbean. In winter (November–March) NE groundswells bring hollow walls and barrels up to 3 m; in summer the trade winds deliver a small wind swell. For learning there are gentle waves on the south coast.
barbados-soup-bowl.rating_basis: Many guides rate it the best wave in the Caribbean, and it is a favourite of Kelly Slater; “works about 355 days a year” (Surfertoday), WSL Barbados Surf Pro events (Perfect Wave, Surf-forecast). Downsides — the trade wind often blows onshore, shallow reef and urchins
barbados-soup-bowl.hazards: Shallow reef and rocks, sea urchins on the inside section, rip currents, powerful waves on big winter swells
barbados-soup-bowl.crowd_note: Crowded line-up on good swells and at weekends, and the locals know the peak; noticeably quieter on weekdays
barbados-soup-bowl.region: East (Atlantic) coast of Barbados, St. Joseph parish
barbados-soup-bowl.area_breaks: Nearby: Parlours (to the south, a fun wave), Box-by-Box and Sunset (to the north), Sandbank (soft beach break, beginners), Duppies (north of the island, big waves); on the south of the island (~30 km) — Freights Bay (left, beginner–intermediate), Surfer's Point, Brandons, South Point
barbados-soup-bowl.beginner_months: At Soup Bowl beginners can only go out on small, windless mornings at low tide. Lessons run year-round on the south coast — Freights Bay, Surfer's Point, Brandons (from June to October southerly and hurricane swells work there), and in winter on the gentle Sandbank north of Bathsheba
pros: One of the best and most consistent waves in the Caribbean
Warm water year-round
Works on any tide
Compact island — lots of spots within an hour's drive
cons: The trade wind often blows side-onshore
Shallow reef and urchins on the inside section
Expensive island
Small on the east coast in summer
barbados-soup-bowl.best_wind_dir: SW–W (offshore); also works in the NE–E trade wind

florianopolis-joaquina.description: Florianópolis (“Floripa”) is an island with 40 beaches and the main surf hub of southern Brazil. Joaquina is a powerful, peaky beach break by the dunes, mostly lefts over sand, very consistent and famous for hosting world tour events. The season is the southern-hemisphere autumn and winter (March–August), when cold fronts bring SE swells and an offshore westerly wind.
florianopolis-joaquina.rating_basis: The surf capital of southern Brazil: Joaquina is a historic world tour venue (1980s–90s), a very consistent beach break (Surf-forecast — “very consistent”, Mondo Surf — “world class”); dozens of beaches on the island suit different winds (Culture Trip, NSC Total). Downsides — crowds, currents and a cold winter
florianopolis-joaquina.hazards: Strong rip currents and a tough paddle-out on big swells, heavy close-outs on the shorebreak, localism on the main peaks, thefts from cars in the car park
florianopolis-joaquina.crowd_note: Joaquina and Praia Mole are often packed, especially at weekends and during the summer holidays (January–February); the island's other beaches — Santinho, Moçambique, Matadeiro — are quieter
florianopolis-joaquina.region: Santa Catarina Island, Santa Catarina state, southern Brazil
florianopolis-joaquina.area_breaks: Nearby: Praia Mole (powerful beach break, ~3 km), Campeche and Campeche Rights (peaks and a right by the island), Barra da Lagoa (beginners, by the channel), Moçambique and Santinho (beach breaks in the northeast), Matadeiro and Lagoinha do Leste (south of the island, work on southerly swells)
florianopolis-joaquina.beginner_months: December–March (warm water, smaller waves): lessons at Barra da Lagoa, Campeche and Lagoinha; at Joaquina beginners should stick to small days
pros: Very consistent waves
Lots of beaches for any wind and level
A well-developed city, safe and inexpensive by Brazilian standards
Surf culture, schools, shapers
cons: Winter water 17–19 °C — a 3/2 wetsuit needed
Crowded main peaks
NE wind dominates in summer
Strong currents

pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.description: Pichilemu is Chile's surf capital on the cold Pacific coast. Punta de Lobos is a powerful left-hand point by the Los Morros rocks that picks up S and SW swells almost year-round: on small days it offers long walls for confident intermediates, and in winter big waves up to 10 m. The water is cold because of the Humboldt Current, but the waves are very consistent.
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.rating_basis: Chile's surf capital and a World Surfing Reserve (2017): Punta de Lobos is a left-hand point up to 800 m long that holds waves up to 8–10 m and hosts the Ceremonial Punta de Lobos big-wave event (Surfertoday, The Surf Atlas, Chile Travel). Downsides — cold water and a tricky entry
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.hazards: Slippery rock shelf when entering from Los Morros, strong current along the point, cold water and hypothermia, rocky headlands; seismic zone — watch for tsunami warnings
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.crowd_note: Punta de Lobos is “never empty”, but several take-off zones spread people out; La Puntilla is packed with schools in summer; quieter in the shoulder seasons (March–May, September–November)
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.region: O'Higgins Region, central coast of Chile (≈200 km from Santiago)
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.area_breaks: Nearby: La Puntilla (long, soft left by the town, all levels), Infiernillo (fast, hollow left over sand, advanced), Diamante (sandy section of Lobos on small days), beach breaks north of Pichilemu (beginners), Cáhuil and Bucalemu to the south
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.beginner_months: November–March: smaller swells and lighter winds — lessons on the gentle La Puntilla left by the Pichilemu waterfront (almost all the schools operate there) and on the beach breaks north of town
pros: Very consistent swells year-round
World-class long left
Waves for every level (La Puntilla)
Friendly locals, surf culture
cons: Cold water 12–16 °C — a 4/3 wetsuit and booties
Tricky entry off the rocks
Storms, rain and huge waves in winter
Far from the airport
pichilemu-punta-de-lobos.best_wind_dir: E–SE (offshore); a light S–SW is OK (the cliffs give shelter)

santa-teresa-mal-pais.description: Santa Teresa and Mal País are several kilometres of peaky beach break with reef slabs on the southern Nicoya Peninsula, open to every Pacific swell. There are waves almost every day: clean 1–1.5 m with offshore wind in the dry season, and powerful S swells up to 2–3 m in the green season. A trendy yoga-and-surf town with good cafés.
santa-teresa-mal-pais.rating_basis: One of the most consistent places in Costa Rica — works almost every day year-round (The Surf Atlas: ~90% of days in the green season); it features in the country's top lists (Surfertoday, Surf-forecast, Lapoint). Downsides in reviews — a dusty dirt road, high prices and growing crowds
santa-teresa-mal-pais.hazards: Strong rip currents, rocks and reef slabs (Playa Carmen, Punta Barrigona, the Hermosa point), heavy close-outs on big swells, quad bikes on the roads
santa-teresa-mal-pais.crowd_note: The main peaks of Santa Teresa and Playa Carmen are crowded, especially in December–April; the long beach lets you find an empty peak, and Mal País and Hermosa are calmer
santa-teresa-mal-pais.region: Nicoya Peninsula (south), Puntarenas province, Pacific Ocean
santa-teresa-mal-pais.area_breaks: Nearby: Playa Carmen (beach break/reef by the crossroads, advanced on big days), Mal País and Punta Barrigona (reefs, hollow waves, from 2 m), La Lora and Suck Rock (peaks on the northern part of the beach), Playa Hermosa (beginners, right-hand point at high tide), Manzanillo (reefs to the north), Playa Grande near Montezuma
santa-teresa-mal-pais.beginner_months: December–April (dry season): smaller waves, offshore all day — lessons at Playa Hermosa and on the inside waves of Santa Teresa, also at Playa Carmen on small days
pros: Waves almost every day year-round
Lots of peaks along a long beach — for all levels
Warm water 27–29 °C
Surf-town atmosphere, schools and camps
cons: Hard to get to (ferry or domestic flight, dirt road)
Expensive accommodation and food
Dust in the dry season, mud and downpours in September–October
Growing crowds
santa-teresa-mal-pais.airport: TMU — Tambor (domestic flights), ~40 min; LIR — Liberia, ~3.5–5 h; SJO — San José, ~5 h including the ferry

tamarindo-playa-grande.description: Tamarindo is a lively resort town in Guanacaste and one of Costa Rica's top places to learn to surf: a soft beach break in front of town, warm water and dozens of schools. More serious waves are close by: Playa Grande across the river mouth, reef peaks and the Estero mouth. In the dry season it's offshore almost all day; in the green season big SW swells arrive.
tamarindo-playa-grande.rating_basis: One of Costa Rica's main surf resorts and the best place to learn in Guanacaste (The Surf Atlas, Witch's Rock Surf Camp, Surf-forecast — “a great spot for beginners”). Playa Grande delivers powerful A-frames for intermediates and up; the downsides are crowds and tourist development
tamarindo-playa-grande.hazards: Crocodiles in the Estero mouth (don't wade across to Playa Grande), reefs and rocks at Pico and Henry's, shallow sandbars at the river mouth, currents; cold upwelling from December
tamarindo-playa-grande.crowd_note: Tamarindo's line-up is one of the most crowded in the country, with lots of schools. Playa Grande, Palmeras and Casitas are noticeably quieter
tamarindo-playa-grande.region: Guanacaste, northern Nicoya Peninsula, Pacific Ocean
tamarindo-playa-grande.area_breaks: Nearby: Playa Grande (powerful A-frames, intermediate+; Palmeras at the north end for beginners), the Estero mouth (fast rights, advanced), Pico Grande and Pico Pequeño (reefs, at high tide), Henry's Left/Right, Capitán Suizo (beginners), Playa Langosta (A-frame, intermediate), Avellanas and Playa Negra (reef, ~20 km); by boat — Witch's Rock and Ollie's Point
tamarindo-playa-grande.beginner_months: Year-round, best in December–April: 0.5–1.5 m waves and offshore wind. Lessons on Tamarindo's main beach, by Capitán Suizo and at Palmeras (north end of Playa Grande)

Close to Liberia airport
Infrastructure, accommodation for every budget

tamarindo-playa-grande.airport: LIR — Liberia, ~1 h 15 min; SJO — San José, ~4.5 h
tamarindo-playa-grande.best_wind_dir: E–NE (offshore, almost all day in the dry season)

montanita-la-punta.description: Montañita is a bohemian surf village on the Ecuadorian coast with waves almost every day. La Punta is a right-hand point over reef and rocks at the north end of the beach: at low tide it breaks faster and barrels, and it holds up to 3–4 m. In front of the village there's a long sandy beach break for beginners. The best time is December–May: warm, sunny and with N swells; summer and autumn are cooler and overcast (garúa).
montanita-la-punta.rating_basis: Ecuador's main surf resort and a venue for national and international contests (Wikipedia “Surfing in Ecuador”, Perfect Wave, Surf-forecast): a playful right over reef and a long beach break. The downsides every review mentions are the crowd on the point with a strict pecking order and the noisy party village
montanita-la-punta.hazards: Rocks and reef at La Punta (especially at low tide), currents on the beach break on big swells, strong equatorial sun, petty theft
montanita-la-punta.crowd_note: La Punta often has 25+ people and a tough queue; on the beach break the peaks spread people out, and Olón, Manglaralto and Ayampe are quieter. Calmer early in the morning and at midday
montanita-la-punta.region: Santa Elena province, Ruta del Spondylus, Pacific coast
montanita-la-punta.area_breaks: Nearby: Montañita beach break (lefts and rights, all levels), Olón (gentle waves, ~10 min north), Manglaralto (beach break to the south), Ayampe (powerful beach break, ~30 km north), Salinas and Puerto Engabao (further south)
montanita-la-punta.beginner_months: Year-round on the sandy beach break in front of the village (2 km of peaks) and at Olón, on mid to high tide; most comfortable in December–May, when it's warm and sunny
pros: Waves almost year-round
Warm water, usually no wetsuit needed
Inexpensive, lots of hostels and schools
Beginner-friendly options nearby
cons: Very crowded on the point, strict pecking order
Noisy party village
June–November is overcast and cooler
Rocks at low tide

fuerteventura-north-shore.description: The north coast of Fuerteventura between Corralejo and El Cotillo is a chain of volcanic reefs along a dirt track known as the “North Shore”. Majanicho is a right-hand reef point in a quiet fishing cove: it holds big swell, and its inside section suits progressing surfers. From October to March there's consistent N swell and water that's warm by European standards; in summer the waves are smaller and strong trade winds blow.
fuerteventura-north-shore.rating_basis: “Europe's Hawaii”: a dozen volcanic reefs along the North Shore (El Hierro, Majanicho, Lobos, Bubble) and a warm winter climate. Thesurfatlas and Surfertoday rank the north of the island among the Canaries' best; downsides — crowds and localism on the best reefs
fuerteventura-north-shore.hazards: Shallow, sharp volcanic reefs and rocks, sea urchins (bring reef booties), strong currents and rips, no lifeguards at the wild spots
fuerteventura-north-shore.crowd_note: Rocky Point, El Hierro and Majanicho get crowded on a good swell, with local crews holding the peak; the remote reefs to the west and the El Cotillo beaches are quieter in winter
fuerteventura-north-shore.area_breaks: Nearby: El Hierro (heavy A-frame reef, experts), Bubble (fast right-hand slab by the rocks, pros), Lobos (long right-hand point on Lobos island, by boat), La Generosa and La Derecha de los Alemanes (reefs), Rocky Point / Punta Elena (Corralejo, intermediate), Flag Beach (beginners), El Cotillo — Piedra Playa and La Escalera (beach breaks), Punta Blanca, La Caleta, Esquinzo
fuerteventura-north-shore.beginner_months: Year-round, but best in April–September: small waves on the El Cotillo beaches (Piedra Playa, Playa del Castillo, La Escalera) and Flag Beach in Corralejo; in winter beginners learn in sheltered coves, and on the North Shore reefs only on the inside sections on small days
pros: Surfing in winter at +20–22 °C — the best winter alternative to the mainland
Lots of reefs and beaches for every level
Short flight from Europe, plenty of surf camps
Warm water year-round (18–23 °C)
cons: Sharp volcanic reefs, urchins, cuts and board dings
Strong trade winds in summer and often windy in winter

fuerteventura-north-shore.airport: FUE — Fuerteventura (Puerto del Rosario), ~35 min to Corralejo

lanzarote-famara-surf.description: Famara is a 6 km beach beneath the sheer Risco de Famara cliffs next to the surf village of Caleta de Famara. The peaky beach break works almost year-round and suits everyone — from first lessons to big winter days. Fifteen minutes away are the reefs of La Santa and El Quemao, some of the most powerful waves in Europe, for advanced surfers and experts.
lanzarote-famara-surf.rating_basis: Lanzarote is called “Europe's Hawaii”: Famara is the island's main “international” spot for all levels (Thesurfatlas), and the El Quemao reef is one of Europe's most powerful barrels, home to the Quemao Class invitational contest. Downside — strong trade winds in summer
lanzarote-famara-surf.hazards: Strong rip currents at Famara, rocks and seaweed at high tide; at La Santa and El Quemao — sharp, shallow volcanic reef, heavy barrels, urchins
lanzarote-famara-surf.crowd_note: Famara has 6 km of beach and lots of school groups, but there's room for everyone; the La Santa reefs get crowded on a good swell and are packed with locals
lanzarote-famara-surf.region: Canary Islands, northwest Lanzarote (Chinijo Natural Park)
lanzarote-famara-surf.area_breaks: Nearby: La Santa (fast, shallow right-hand reef, confident surfers), El Quemao (heavy left-hand barrel over sharp reef, experts only), San Juan (left-hand reef, advanced), Jameos del Agua (left-hand point on the east coast, localism), La Graciosa island
lanzarote-famara-surf.beginner_months: Year-round, best in May–September: on Famara beach the waves are smaller and schools run daily; in winter, when the swell is big, beginners are taken to a training beach 10 minutes away. La Santa and El Quemao are for experienced surfers only
pros: Year-round surf, warm winter (+21–23 °C)
Huge beach for all levels
World-class reefs nearby for experienced surfers
Lots of schools and camps, including some with lessons in Russian
cons: Strong cross-shore wind (trade wind), especially in summer
Currents and rips at Famara
The La Santa reefs are sharp and shallow
You need a car, the village is small

mundaka.description: A legendary left-hand barrel on a sandbar at the mouth of the Oka river by the fishing village of Mundaka. On perfect days it offers a fast take-off, a long barrel and rides of up to 200 m, but the wave is fickle: it needs a big NW swell, a southerly wind and low tide. Dredging in 2005 wiped out the sandbar, but it has since recovered.
mundaka.rating_basis: One of the best river-mouth lefts in the world: the Billabong Pro Mundaka world championship event (since 1999), barrels and rides of up to 200 m (Surfertoday, Thesurfatlas). Downside — it's fickle: by estimates it only works 50–70 days a year
mundaka.hazards: A very strong current out of the river mouth that sweeps you out to sea (especially on the tide), a shallow sandbar and heavy barrels, crowds and localism
mundaka.crowd_note: On the rare perfect days surfers come from all over the region, and the line-up is packed and very competitive
mundaka.region: Basque Country (Biscay), Urdaibai Biosphere Reserve, Bay of Biscay
mundaka.area_breaks: Nearby: Laga (forgiving beach break for intermediates), Bakio (beach break over rocks, picks up more swell, some localism), Sopelana and Meñakoz (35–40 km, near Bilbao)
mundaka.beginner_months: Mundaka itself is off-limits for beginners. In summer and early autumn they learn at Laga beach (across the estuary) and at Bakio (25 min); Laga also suits intermediates preparing for Mundaka
pros: A world-class wave — one of the best lefts in Europe
Picturesque Basque village and the Urdaibai reserve
Laga and Bakio nearby when Mundaka isn't working
cons: Rarely works (50–70 days a year)
Advanced surfers only
Heavy localism and crowds on good days
Almost always flat in summer

zarautz.description: Zarautz is the longest beach in the Basque Country and the unofficial surf capital of Gipuzkoa, 20 minutes from San Sebastián. Several sandbars produce peaks breaking both ways: softer and smaller in the west, steep take-offs and barrels in the east. It suits almost everyone: there are schools on the beach, and on a big swell the wave holds up to 3–4 m.
zarautz.rating_basis: Thesurfatlas: “one of the best beach breaks in Spain”, a great place for learning and intermediates; Surf-forecast calls it a “very consistent” spot. It hosts WSL events (Pro Zarautz). The wave isn't legendary but it's reliable, and San Sebastián is next door
zarautz.hazards: Rip currents on big swells, crowds and schools in the line-up, water pollution after rain (noted by Surf-forecast)
zarautz.crowd_note: The long beach (2.5 km) with several peaks spreads people out, but it's busy in season and at weekends; it gets more popular every year
zarautz.area_breaks: Nearby: Zurriola in San Sebastián (20 km, beach break — gentle waves by the Kursaal, a powerful peak by the Sagüés wall), Getaria, Zumaia (Itzurun, one of the most consistent spots in the north), Deba (lefts by the jetty), Mundaka (70 km, pros)
zarautz.beginner_months: May–September: summer is the best time to learn (0.5–1.5 m waves, water up to 22 °C); beginners surf the western, more sheltered part of the beach. In San Sebastián lessons are held at Zurriola by the Kursaal

Great for learning and intermediates

zarautz.airport: BIO — Bilbao, ~1 h (85 km); BIQ — Biarritz, ~45 min; EAS — San Sebastián, ~35 min

biarritz-cote-des-basques.description: Biarritz is an elegant resort and the birthplace of European surfing. Côte des Basques is a long beach below the cliffs: soft waves for longboarding and learning in the north, more power in the south. It works mainly at low and mid tide; at high tide the beach disappears under water. Nearby are the Anglet beaches, the Guéthary reefs and Hossegor, 30 minutes away.
biarritz-cote-des-basques.rating_basis: The cradle of European surfing (1957) and a longboard mecca; surf-report.com calls it “the biggest beach break in Biarritz”, for all levels. The waves are average by world standards, but the mix of city, climate and dozens of beaches within 20 km makes Biarritz one of Europe's most popular surf destinations
biarritz-cote-des-basques.hazards: Rocks at the foot of the cliffs at high tide, powerful currents at Marbella, crowds and schools in the line-up
biarritz-cote-des-basques.crowd_note: Very crowded in summer and at weekends, lots of schools; quieter in autumn and on the Anglet beaches
biarritz-cote-des-basques.region: French Basque Country, Nouvelle-Aquitaine (Bay of Biscay)
biarritz-cote-des-basques.area_breaks: Nearby: Grande Plage (town beach, all levels), Marbella (powerful waves and currents, experienced surfers), Milady (all levels, bodyboarding), Ilbarritz, the Anglet beaches (Les Cavaliers, La Barre — 4 km of beach breaks), the reefs of Guéthary (Parlementia) and Lafitenia 10–15 km to the south
biarritz-cote-des-basques.beginner_months: April–October: beginners learn at the north end of Côte des Basques by Villa Belza (soft waves, longboarding) and on Grande Plage at low tide; in summer the waves are small and the water warm — ideal for first lessons

City infrastructure, airport 10 minutes away
Lots of spots within 20 km — from beaches to reefs
Warm water in summer and early autumn
cons: Waves are mostly average, often small in summer
Doesn't work on all tides, the beach vanishes at high tide
Crowded in summer
Expensive accommodation

hossegor-la-graviere.description: Hossegor is the centre of French surfing on the endless sandy beaches of the Landes. The Capbreton submarine canyon and the sandbars produce powerful world-class barrels at La Gravière and La Nord, while a couple of kilometres away there are calm beaches for learning. The best time is September–November: big swell, warm water and fewer people.
hossegor-la-graviere.rating_basis: Europe's surf capital: a long-running world championship venue (Quiksilver Pro France), and La Gravière is one of the most powerful beach-break barrels in the world. Thesurfatlas calls September–October the “golden period”; on Surf-forecast October is the best month
hossegor-la-graviere.hazards: Powerful shorebreak and barrels over shallow sandbars, very strong rip currents (especially at La Gravière and on a big swell), crowds in the line-up
hossegor-la-graviere.crowd_note: In July–August (French holidays) the line-ups are packed, and La Sud is swarming with schools; quieter in autumn and on weekdays, and on the beaches of Seignosse and the Landes further north you can find an empty peak
hossegor-la-graviere.area_breaks: Nearby: Les Culs Nus (fast barrelling wave, intermediate and up), La Nord (big wave in winter), La Centrale and La Sud (beginners), Les Estagnots and Le Penon in Seignosse (powerful peaks), Capbreton (La Piste, Le Santocha), Labenne and Les Bourdaines
hossegor-la-graviere.beginner_months: May–September: lessons on La Sud beach in Hossegor (sheltered small waves) and on the beaches of Capbreton and Seignosse; La Gravière is off-limits for beginners in any season

Dozens of peaks along the beaches — you can always find your own
A developed surf industry: schools, camps, shapers, outlets
Warm water in late summer and autumn

newquay-fistral.description: Fistral in Newquay is Britain's main surf beach, facing straight into the Atlantic. The sandy beach break holds waves up to 3–4 m: rights at the north end, lefts at the south. For intermediates the season is autumn, when the water is still warm and the first groundswells arrive; winter brings cold water and storms, summer small waves for learning.
newquay-fistral.rating_basis: The UK's surf capital: Fistral is Cornwall's best-known surf beach and the venue for the Boardmasters festival and pro contests; Thesurfatlas — “reliable quality rights” at North Fistral. By world standards the wave is average and the water cold
newquay-fistral.hazards: Strong rip currents along the rocks at the south end of the beach, rocks at Little Fistral at high tide, cold water (risk of hypothermia), crowds
newquay-fistral.crowd_note: Fistral is always busy, and in summer the neighbouring beaches have “literally hundreds” of students; quieter in autumn and on weekdays, with empty peaks on the beaches north and south of Newquay
newquay-fistral.area_breaks: Nearby: North Fistral (rights), South Fistral (lefts, better at high tide), Little Fistral (hollow wedges over rocks, at low tide), the Cribbar (big wave off Towan Head, experts), Towan and Great Western (beginners), Crantock (river mouth), Watergate Bay, Harlyn and Polzeath (further north)
newquay-fistral.beginner_months: May–September: lessons on the town beaches of Towan and Great Western (sheltered, a “beginners' mecca”) and on Fistral on small days; in summer a 3/2 or 2 mm wetsuit is enough

A developed surf industry and plenty of schools
Beginner beaches nearby and alternatives in any wind
Newquay airport 15 minutes away
